units.translation: the political reference to the alliance between Athens and Argos is unmistakable; see also already vv. 289 ff.; 671 ff. Here, however, unlike at 671, the talk is chiefly negative, about the avoidance of all hostility, already at 765 f., but developed in vv. 767 ff., which Dindorf considers a later interpolation. If, however, one follows him in excising 767–774, the oath becomes not only very short but also unclear: he has sworn that no Argive will ever march against Athens; but how can he guarantee such a thing? To this, 767 ff. give an answer, but according to Dindorf none. Thus the excision is untenable, and whoever thinks of the times of the Peloponnesian War as being in the author's mind thereby posits a completely impossible confusion of Argos and Sparta. Since, then, the historical Argives never thought of a campaign against Athens, the poet in fact keeps himself at the height proper to him, above contemporary history and momentary interests. Euripides does similarly in the Suppliants 1187 ff., where Adrastus swears the oath for Argos, and where in place of 767 ff. there stands a curse upon the Argives in case of breach.
⟦1⟧ 763 only here; ⟦2⟧ only ⟦3⟧, see on that passage; the -⟦4⟧ has lost its force, and the sense is approximately = ⟦5⟧.

doloisi kekasmene (you who are furnished with wiles)
phrourais kekastai dexiais te doryphorōn (he is furnished with garrisons and the right hands of spearmen)
panourgiais meizosi kekasmenon (furnished with greater villainies)
pyrgon stegein euchesthe polemion dory (pray that the tower may ward off the enemy spear)
